accessibility.text: “The necessity of holding the resurrection arises from this — that man may obtain the last end for which he was made. This cannot be accomplished in this life, nor in the life of the separated soul …  it is necessary for the selfsame man to rise again; and this is effected by the selfsame soul being united to the selfsame body. For otherwise there would be no resurrection properly speaking, if the same man were not reformed.”
Is life after death possible?
Matters are less clear when it comes to our other answers to the survival question.

But we also saw that if this is true, Original Ship ≠ Reconstructed Ship. And if this is so, that would seem to imply that if a material thing breaks into its constituent parts, reassembling those parts does not bring the original material thing back into existence.
This is also implied by the use of the word “resurrection” — if life after death were simply the continued existence of an immaterial soul, then there would be nothing needing to be “raised up.”
These views differ in important ways, but they all agree that your survival depends on the survival of a certain physical thing.
And that seems to imply that, even if God did reassemble the parts which formerly composed some body (or brain), that would not be enough to bring that very body (or brain) back into existence.
How can we make sense of this idea, given obvious facts about the decay of bodies and brains after death?

Views of this kind face an obvious problem in making sense of the possibility of life after death. After death bodies decay (or are cremated). Doesn’t that just show that the relevant physical objects won’t survive your death — and so that, if one of the above views is right, you won’t?
This is a serious problem for the idea of “resurrection as reassembly.” Is there any other way to make sense of the idea of a bodily resurrection?

One idea (defended by Aquinas and others) is that at the time of resurrection our bodies could be reassembled by God. While it is true that our bodies decay after death, the material of which they were composed does not cease to exist. Surely an omnipotent being could then simply reassemble our bodies out of the matter from which they were composed when we were living.

This is a problem which has long troubled philosophers in the Christian tradition.
Would this be enough for God to bring our bodies back into existence?
organism survival:  X is me just in case X is the same organism as me
This might sound surprising. After all, don’t Christians believe that one’s immaterial soul is enough for life after death?
psychological survival:  X is me just in case X stands in the right psychological connections to me
